boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Nienburg entry (capitulation, 26 November 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: the Prussian garrison of the fortress under its commandant, General Strachwitz, and General Savary's troops before it, from Savary's march from Hameln and the approach of the first patrols on 24 November through the summons and the negotiation of the 25th to the fall of the place on the 26th. The fortress's restoration from 1803, the earlier summons by a division of Mortier's corps, the French orders to observe Hameln and Nienburg, and the suspension of arms of 16 November, which was not ratified, are context. Hameln (B376d), which Savary's troops took before moving on Nienburg, is outside this entry. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) as 6,000 men under General of Division Savary, and side B (Prussian) as the garrison of 3,000 men with 51 guns under Major General v. Strachwitz, which the French forced to capitulate without a stroke of the sword, after which the garrison fell into captivity as prisoners of war. By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner gives the garrison's parts and total (claim side-b-strength), the Emperor and Mortier other estimates (claim side-b-strength-french), and Höpfner and the French letters side A's troops (claim side-a-strength). Bodart's 3,000 is Höpfner's 2911 rounded up, and his 51 guns are Höpfner's 39 cannon, 10 howitzers and 2 mortars, without the 12 Wallbüchsen (our comparison and arithmetic). His 6,000 for side A is the figure he prints for Savary's force at Hameln (B376d; our comparison); no passage read gives a total for side A at Nienburg. Which source Bodart used was not checked. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 26/11. capitulation of Nienburg'; 'the French (6,000 men) under General of Division Savary force the Prussian garrison (3,000 men, 51 guns) under Major General v. Strachwitz to capitulate without a stroke of the sword, after which the garrison fell into captivity as prisoners of war'.

claims.value: Side A (French): Bodart gives 6,000 men under General of Division Savary. The 32nd Bulletin, of 16 November: Savary had been charged with the blockade of Hameln with the Dutch division. Höpfner: on 22 November two more French regiments arrived at Hameln with some 10-pounder howitzers, probably taken somewhere in Hesse; Savary, after leaving a garrison of 100 French and 150 Dutch at Hameln, set out on both banks of the Weser against Nienburg, so that on the 24th the first enemy patrols approached the town; on the 25th Savary, accompanied by General Schramm and several officers, was fetched in by the commandant. Earlier, a division of Mortier's corps marching past had summoned the fortress. Mortier wrote on 13 November that he was ordering Dumonceau to leave in observation, both before Hameln and before Nienburg, the 2nd and 3rd light infantry regiments, the 7th of the line and the 2nd of cavalry, all Dutch troops, weak corps whose return he had not yet obtained, with 10 pieces of ordnance. No passage read gives a return of side A before Nienburg.
claims.rationale: Bodart from the frame transcription; Höpfner and the French letters read from the page images, the figures checked on full-resolution crops. The force before Nienburg was the one Savary led from Hameln, whose composition and strength the passages read do not give; it followed Savary's dispositions after the capitulation of Hameln and orders the passages read do not give, so the phase is left unresolved. Bodart's 6,000 is the figure he prints for Savary's force at Hameln (B376d; our comparison), and is not shown to be a count. The passages read do not say whether the two regiments or the howitzers that reached Hameln on 22 November went on to Nienburg, whether Mortier's observation troops of 13 November stood before Nienburg when Savary came, or when the division of Mortier's corps passed and summoned it. claims.value: Höpfner: a division of Mortier's corps marching past had earlier summoned the fortress, and was refused. General Savary, leaving a garrison of 100 French and 150 Dutch at Hameln, set out on both banks of the Weser against Nienburg, and the first patrols approached the town on the 24th. On the evening of 24 November a parlementaire of Savary's brought the summons to surrender, with an account of all the Prussian army's well-known misfortunes and the remark that insignificant Nienburg was incapable of any defence; a second parlementaire, General Schramm, who came soon after, sought to prove to the commandant that the conditions he had sent could not possibly be granted him, but invited him to a verbal discussion with Savary. On the 25th at 9 in the morning the commandant fetched in Savary, accompanied by Schramm and several officers, and for over an hour urged him in vain to grant the garrison free withdrawal; the French Captain Semery drew up the points of the capitulation with Major Dreßler.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, read from the page images of pp. 378 and 380-382. These were the steps of side A's commanders before Nienburg, so the claim is tagged commander-created. Höpfner gives the summons and Schramm's argument in summary and cites no document for them in the passages read; the commandant's conditions are in claim side-b-command. Who commanded the division of Mortier's corps that summoned the fortress earlier, and when, is not stated in the passages read. claims.value: Höpfner: the commandant, Major General Strachwitz, had had rows of palisades set on the berm before the curtains and ladders fixed in the re-entrant angles, to make up for the lack of a covered way and of posterns; he had shown himself very active in arming the fortress, had rejected the earlier summons of a division of Mortier's corps marching past, and had not even admitted to his presence the deputation of the Hanoverian Landes-Kollegium that called at Nienburg from Hameln. To Savary's summons of the 24th the commandant, in the presence of Majors Colson and Dreßler, rejected all proposals, but sent word that he was inclined to capitulate if granted a three-week armistice and then free withdrawal to the King's army; he accepted Schramm's invitation to a discussion with Savary and fixed it for the next day. He then called to a council of war, besides those named, the commanders of the 3rd musketeer battalions, Lieutenant Colonels Schönowski and Brandenstein, both well into their sixties, and Major Gordon. All the staff officers held it advisable to surrender on advantageous terms, since a bombardment would quickly turn the town into a heap of ashes, and Colson and Captain Geyling especially described the fortress's state as desperate, since besides fire the frost, perhaps soon to set in, was to be feared, when the ditches would freeze and the enemy would grant no capitulation at all; Colson, also weighing the general situation of the state, declared it wholly useless to defend Nienburg under the circumstances. All the officers present then agreed to the surrender and signed the protocol of the proceedings; Strachwitz meant to put the condition of free withdrawal once more but believed from the outset that it would not be granted. On the 25th, after urging it on Savary in vain for over an hour, he charged Major Dreßler to draw up the points of the capitulation with the French Captain Semery, which was done with Major Colson and Lieutenants Bismark of the regiment Prinz Ferdinand and Longe de Beauveset of the regiment Wedell. Officers of the garrison came and went during the negotiations, most of the commanders having given notice the evening before that there would be a capitulation; no one was found who opposed it, the general misfortune and the idea that Nienburg could not be held having struck down every energetic resolve from the outset. Höpfner's judgement: even if a speedy fall was to be foreseen once the enemy made serious preparations, such preparations should at least have been awaited, since with the enemy's light field guns neither sluices nor batardeaus could be so easily destroyed nor the town set on fire if the fortress's heavy calibres kept the enemy at the proper distance.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 380-383. These were the decisions of the commandant and his council, so the claim is tagged commander-created. Höpfner cites no document for the council or its protocol in the passages read, and the judgement is his own. The council's fear that a bombardment would turn the town to ashes stands beside Höpfner's description, in which a road 30 paces wide between the wall and the buildings meant that the burning of the town did not hinder the defence (claim nienburg-ground); both are kept. English renderings (ours): 'the commandant, Major General Strachwitz, had had rows of palisades set on the berm before the curtains, and ladders for climbing up fixed in the re-entrant angles at the revetment, to make up for the lack of a covered way and of posterns'; 'General Strachwitz had shown himself very active in arming the fortress, had rejected the earlier summons of a division of Mortier's corps marching past, and had not even admitted to his presence the deputation of the Hanoverian Landes-Kollegium [provincial government], which called at Nienburg from Hameln'; 'on the evening of 24 November a parlementaire of General Savary's brought the summons to surrender, with an account of all the well-known misfortunes of the Prussian army attached, and with the remark that insignificant Nienburg was surely incapable of any defence'; 'the commandant, in the presence of Majors Colson and Dreßler, the latter of whom did the duty of town major, rejected all proposals, but had General Savary told that he was inclined to capitulate if he were granted a three-week armistice and then free withdrawal to the King's army'; 'a second parlementaire, General Schramm, arriving soon afterwards, sought to prove to the commandant that such conditions could not possibly be granted him, but invited him to a verbal discussion with General Savary'; 'General Strachwitz accepted the offer and fixed the following day for it'; 'after General Schramm had left the fortress, the commandant called together to a council of war, besides the persons named above, the commanders of the 3rd musketeer battalions; they were Lieutenant Colonels Schönowski and Brandenstein, both well into their sixties, and Major Gordon'; 'all the staff officers were of the opinion that it was advisable to surrender to the enemy on advantageous terms, since a bombardment would quickly turn the town into a heap of ashes; 'Major Colson also took the general situation of the state into consideration, and declared that under the prevailing circumstances it was wholly useless to defend Nienburg'; 'all the officers present thereupon agreed to the surrender and signed the protocol of the proceedings'; claims.value: Bodart records the capitulation of Nienburg on 26 November: the French under Savary forced the Prussian garrison under Major General v. Strachwitz to capitulate without a stroke of the sword, after which the garrison fell into captivity as prisoners of war. Höpfner: on the 25th, after the commandant had urged Savary in vain to grant free withdrawal, Major Dreßler and the French Captain Semery drew up the points of the capitulation; after the parole it was made known and the bridgehead handed over to the enemy at once, while the walls stayed occupied by the Prussians until the morning of the 26th. In the night to the 26th some burghers broke open and plundered the magazines, and a young artillery officer on his own authority destroyed a great part of the munition stores to keep them from the enemy. The officers were released on their word of honour, and the Feldwebel, some non-commissioned officers and married soldiers released home with passes; all Westphalians among the soldiers were to be taken only to Minden and released from there; the remaining, but small, body of men was taken to France; the officers kept their horses and other property, the men their knapsacks. So on 26 November Nienburg too fell into the enemy's hands without any defence; with it fell, Silesia excepted, Prussia's last strong point on the left bank of the Oder. The Emperor wrote to the Grand Duke of Berg from Posen on 3 December that Glogau had surrendered and that the place of Nienburg had likewise surrendered.

claims.value: Bodart places Nienburg, a town in Prussia, province of Hanover, on the right bank of the Weser, 45 km north-west of Hanover. Höpfner: Nienburg, on the right bank of the Weser, had been largely razed soon after the Seven Years' War, but was to some extent put in order again for defence in 1803, when the French took possession of Hanover. The fortress formed a triangle whose southern side was washed by a small river, the Aue, which filled the ditches and flooded its whole left bank as soon as the mill on the south side of the fortress, between the town and the hornwork, was shut off, so that only the northern side, between the Weser and the inundation, remained open to a regular attack; the two places of arms on the wings of that front were overlooked from the heights before it. A ravelin served as bridgehead on the left bank of the Weser, and the valley heights overlooked it. The town was narrow and badly built, mostly of half-timbered houses, so that a bombardment could soon lay it in ashes; but since a road 30 paces wide ran between the wall and the buildings where the Weser and the inundation did not secure the place, the burning of the town did not hinder the defence. Savary's troops approached on both banks of the Weser.
claims.rationale: Location and works as described, read from the page images. No plan of Nienburg was inspected, and where each work stood is taken only from Höpfner's description; the works themselves are in claim fortification. 'Geschützt', of the mill, is read as the closing of its sluice gates (our reading). Höpfner gives the road's width in paces; it is not converted. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(town in Prussia, province of Hanover, on the right bank of the Weser, 45 km north-west of Hanover)'; 'Nienburg, situated on the right bank of the Weser, had been for the most part razed soon after the Seven Years' War, but in 1803, when the French took possession of Hanover, had been to some' (the word 'einigermaßen', to some extent, continues on p. 379); 'extent put in order again for defence' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 378); 'accordingly the fortress formed a triangle, whose southern side was washed by a small river, the Aue, which filled the ditches and flooded its whole left bank as soon as the mill on the south side of the fortress, between the town and the hornwork, was shut off' ('geschützt', read as the closing of the mill's sluice gates; our reading); 'thus only the northern side of the triangle, between the Weser and the inundation, remained for a regular attack'; 'a continuous covered way did not exist, but only two places of arms on the wings of the front, overlooked from the heights lying before it, and between the middle bastions a ravelin covering the Norder gate'; 'a ravelin with wet ditches and a well-palisaded covered way served as bridgehead on the left bank of the Weser; the valley heights, however, overlooked the bridgehead, against which cover had been sought by bonnets and traverses'; 'the town was narrow and badly built, consisting mostly of half-timbered houses, so that it could soon be laid in ashes by a bombardment; but since a road 30 paces wide ran between the wall and the buildings where the Weser and the inundation did not secure the place, the defence was not hindered by the burning of the town'; 'General Savary, after leaving a garrison of 100 Frenchmen and 150 Dutch, set out on both banks of the Weser against Nienburg, so that on the 24th the first enemy patrols approached that town'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: a supply of munitions and provisions for more than 3 weeks was stored bombproof, and the commandant's building and the hospital were covered in the same way, though by report only weakly; each main work had small bombproof shelters. There were 39 cannon of all calibres, 10 howitzers, 2 mortars and 12 Wallbüchsen, thus a sufficient number for the fortress. At the council of war Colson and Geyling feared, besides fire, the frost, perhaps soon to set in, when the ditches would freeze. In the night to the 26th some burghers broke open and plundered the magazines, and a young artillery officer destroyed a great part of the munition stores. Side A (French): on 22 November two French regiments arrived at Hameln with some 10-pounder howitzers, probably taken in Hesse; Mortier wrote on 13 November that he was also leaving Dumonceau, with the troops left in observation before Hameln and Nienburg, 10 pieces of ordnance. Höpfner's judgement speaks of the enemy's light field guns and of the fortress's heavy calibres.
claims.rationale: Höpfner and Mortier's letter, read from the page images, the figures checked on full-resolution crops. Side B's guns and stores were set before Savary's approach; side A's guns came from its commanders' dispositions; one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. Höpfner's guns make 51 without the 12 Wallbüchsen (our arithmetic), Bodart's 51 (claim bodart-strength). Höpfner does not say for how many men the 3 weeks' supply was reckoned. Whether the howitzers that reached Hameln or Mortier's 10 pieces came before Nienburg is not shown. No passage read counts the stores found at the capitulation. English renderings (ours): 'a supply of munitions and provisions for more than 3 weeks was stored bombproof; in the same way, though by report only weakly, the commandant's building and the hospital were also covered'; 'each main work had small bombproof shelters'; 'of guns there were 39 cannon of all calibres, 10 howitzers, 2 mortars and 12 Wallbüchsen [rampart guns], thus a sufficient number for the fortress'; 'all the staff officers were of the opinion that it was advisable to surrender to the enemy on advantageous terms, since a bombardment would quickly turn the town into a heap of ashes; but Major Colson and Captain Geyling especially described the state of the fortress as desperate, since besides fire the frost, perhaps soon to set in, was also to be feared, when the ditches would freeze and the enemy would grant no capitulation at all'; 'in the night to the 26th some burghers broke open the magazines and plundered them, and a young artillery officer on his own authority destroyed a great part of the munition stores, to withdraw them from the enemy'; 'on 22 November two more French regiments arrived at Hameln with some 10-pounder howitzers, probably taken somewhere in Hesse'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 13 November 1806'; 'I am giving orders for General Dumonceau to leave in observation, both before Hameln and before Nienburg, the 2nd and 3rd light infantry regiments, the 7th of the line, the 2nd of cavalry, all Dutch troops'; 'these corps, whose return I have not yet been able to obtain, are weak. I am also leaving him 10 pieces of ordnance'; 'even if a speedy fall was to be foreseen once the enemy made serious preparations, such preparations should at least have been awaited first, since with the enemy's light field guns neither sluices nor batardeaus could be so easily destroyed, nor the town set on' (the sentence continues on p. 383); 'fire, if the heavy calibres of the fortress kept the enemy at the proper distance' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 382).

claims.value: Side A (French): the Emperor wrote to the King of Holland on 22 October that the Prussians did not have 1,500 men of garrison at Nienburg on the Weser, and on 31 October that Hameln and Nienburg would not be slow to surrender when they learned of their country's disasters; Mortier wrote on 13 November that the enemy's forces at Hameln and Nienburg were estimated at 10,000 men. claims.rationale: Side A's letters, read from the page images, with Höpfner's. The passages read do not show what side A knew of the garrison's strength, works or stores at Nienburg, or what it learned on entering the town; the Emperor's 'not 1,500' and Mortier's 10,000 are also in claim side-b-strength-french. English renderings (ours): 'the Emperor to the King of Holland. Dessau, 22 October 1806'; 'the Prussians do not have 1,500 men of garrison at Nienburg on the Weser. I have reason to think that they have at Hameln only just what is necessary for the garrison'; 'the Emperor to the King of Holland. Berlin, 31 October 1806'; 'Hameln and Nienburg will not be slow to surrender when they learn of the disasters of their country. Put a small corps of observation before them, without blockading them, to prevent them from making raids in the country'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 13 November 1806'; 'the enemy's forces both at Hameln and at Nienburg are estimated at 10,000 men; they could intercept our convoys and our detachments if they were not closely observed'; 'on the evening of 24 November a parlementaire of General Savary's brought the summons to surrender, with an account of all the well-known misfortunes of the Prussian army attached, and with the remark that insignificant Nienburg was surely incapable of any defence'; 'on the 25th at 9 o'clock in the morning the commandant fetched' (the sentence continues on p. 382; 'holte ... ein', went out to meet and brought in); 'General Savary, who was accompanied by General Schramm and several officers, in, and led him to the Kommandantur [the commandant's headquarters]' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 381).

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: the commandant did not even admit to his presence the deputation of the Hanoverian Landes-Kollegium that called at Nienburg from Hameln. Savary's summons of 24 November came with an account of all the Prussian army's well-known misfortunes; at the council of war Colson took the general situation of the state into consideration; and, Höpfner says, the general misfortune and the idea that Nienburg could not be held struck down every energetic resolve from the outset.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images. The passages read do not show whether the garrison knew of Hameln's capitulation of 20 November or of the suspension of arms of 16 November, whose article 4 named Hameln and Nienburg (claim side-a-objectives), what the Hanoverian deputation came to say, or what side B knew of Savary's strength; Höpfner calls the Prussian army's misfortunes well known without saying when the garrison learned of them. claims.value: Side A (French): on 31 October the Emperor wrote to the King of Holland that Hameln and Nienburg would not be slow to surrender when they learned of their country's disasters, and that he should put a small corps of observation before them, without blockading them, to keep them from raiding the country; on 7 November he told Mortier to leave a small corps before Hameln and Nienburg and to move into Lauenburg and on Hamburg, from where, according to the orders the Emperor would send, Mortier would move into Swedish Pomerania in pursuit of Blücher's column. Mortier wrote on 12 November that he would leave two small corps to observe Hameln and Nienburg as the Emperor prescribed, and on 13 November that he was ordering Dumonceau to leave troops in observation before both. The suspension of arms signed at Charlottenburg on 16 November, which the 33rd Bulletin, of 17 November, prints, provided in article 4 that Hameln and Nienburg, with the places named in article 2, would be handed over to the French troops with their armament and munitions within the eight days following the exchange of ratifications, their garrisons not to be prisoners of war but directed on Kœnigsberg; ratifications were to be exchanged at Graudenz at the latest on the 21st, and by Foucart's note hostilities were to cease only then. The 35th Bulletin, of 28 November, says the King of Prussia told Duroc at Osterode that he could not ratify it. Höpfner: after Hameln, Savary set out against Nienburg; his summons of 24 November said that insignificant Nienburg was incapable of any defence, Schramm argued that the commandant's conditions could not be granted, and on the 25th the commandant's urging could not move Savary to grant the garrison free withdrawal.
claims.rationale: The Emperor's and Mortier's letters and the Bulletins, read from the page images, with Höpfner. The aims moved from observation without blockade (31 October to 13 November) to Savary's summons and his refusal of free withdrawal (24 and 25 November); they came from the Emperor and from the commanders, so the phase is left unresolved. No order for the move against Nienburg was read. The capitulation made the garrison prisoners of war by Bodart, or released most of it by Höpfner (claim side-b-losses), while the suspension, had it been ratified, would have sent it to Kœnigsberg (our comparison); the passages read do not show whether Savary or the garrison knew of the suspension. The sentence on hostilities is Foucart's note, not the suspension's text. English renderings (ours): 'the Emperor to the King of Holland. Berlin, 31 October 1806'; 'Hameln and Nienburg will not be slow to surrender when they learn of the disasters of their country. Put a small corps of observation before them, without blockading them, to prevent them from making raids in the country'; 'the Emperor to Marshal Mortier. Berlin, 7 November 1806'; 'you will leave a small corps before Hameln and Nienburg and will move into Lauenburg and from there on Hamburg, from where, according to the orders I would send you, you would move into Swedish Pomerania in pursuit of General Blücher's column'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 12 November 1806'; 'I shall leave two small corps to observe Hameln and Nienburg as you prescribe to me'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 13 November 1806'; 'I am giving orders for General Dumonceau to leave in observation, both before Hameln and before Nienburg, the 2nd and 3rd light infantry regiments, the 7th of the line, the 2nd of cavalry, all Dutch troops'; '1. 33rd Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 17 November 1806' (the '1.' is the footnote's mark); 'the attached suspension of arms was signed yesterday at Charlottenburg'; 'Art. 4. — The places of Hameln and Nienburg, as well as those designated in article 2, shall be handed over to the French troops with their armament and munitions, of which an inventory shall be drawn up, within the eight days following the exchange of the ratifications of the present suspension of arms. The garrisons of these places shall not be prisoners of war; they shall be directed on Kœnigsberg, and they shall be given every facility necessary for this'; 'Art. 6. — The present suspension of arms shall be ratified by the two high contracting powers, and the exchange of ratifications shall take place at Graudenz at the latest on the 21st of the present month'; 'done at Charlottenburg, 16 November 1806'; 'hostilities were to cease only at the moment of the exchange of ratifications'; '35th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Posen, 28 November 1806'; 'the marshal of the palace, Duroc, went as far as Osterode, where he saw the King of Prussia, who declared to him that part of his states was occupied by the Russians and that he was entirely in their dependence; that consequently he could not ratify the suspension of arms that his plenipotentiaries had concluded, because he could not carry out its stipulations'; 'General Savary, after leaving a garrison of 100 Frenchmen and 150 Dutch, set out on both banks of the Weser against Nienburg, so that on the 24th the first enemy patrols approached that town'; 'on the evening of 24 November a parlementaire of General Savary's brought the summons to surrender, with an account of all the well-known misfortunes of the Prussian army attached, and with the remark that insignificant Nienburg was surely incapable of any defence'; 'a second parlementaire, General Schramm, arriving soon afterwards, sought to prove to the commandant that such conditions could not possibly be granted him, but invited him to a verbal discussion with General Savary'; 'on the 25th at 9 o'clock in the morning the commandant fetched' (the sentence continues on p. 382; 'holte ... ein', went out to meet and brought in); 'General Savary, who was accompanied by General Schramm and several officers, in, and led him to the Kommandantur [the commandant's headquarters]' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 381); 'for over an hour General Strachwitz strove to move General Savary to grant the garrison free withdrawal, but since all urging was in vain, he charged Major Dreßler to draw up the points of the capitulation with the French Captain Semery, which was then done with the participation of Major Colson and of Lieutenants Bismark of the regiment Prinz Ferdinand and Longe de Beauveset of the regiment Wedell'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: when Prussia took possession of the country it was decided to restore the works so far that Nienburg could serve as a secure crossing over the Weser and withstand a three-week siege. To Savary's summons the commandant rejected all proposals but sent word that he was inclined to capitulate if granted a three-week armistice and then free withdrawal to the King's army; the council of war held it advisable to surrender to the enemy on advantageous terms, and Colson declared it wholly useless under the circumstances to defend Nienburg. Strachwitz meant to put the condition of free withdrawal once more, and on the 25th urged it on Savary in vain for over an hour.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images. The aims moved from a defence able to withstand a three-week siege to capitulation on the best terms obtainable; they came from the decision on the works and from the commandant and his council, so the phase is left unresolved. The passages read give no order to the garrison after Jena. English renderings (ours): 'when Prussia took possession of the country it was decided to restore the fortifications so far that Nienburg could serve as a secure crossing over the Weser and withstand a three-week siege'; 'the commandant, in the presence of Majors Colson and Dreßler, the latter of whom did the duty of town major, rejected all proposals, but had General Savary told that he was inclined to capitulate if he were granted a three-week armistice and then free withdrawal to the King's army'; 'all the staff officers were of the opinion that it was advisable to surrender to the enemy on advantageous terms, since a bombardment would quickly turn the town into a heap of ashes; but Major Colson and Captain Geyling especially described the state of the fortress as desperate, since besides fire the frost, perhaps soon to set in, was also to be feared, when the ditches would freeze and the enemy would grant no capitulation at all'; 'Major Colson also took the general situation of the state into consideration, and declared that under the prevailing circumstances it was wholly useless to defend Nienburg'; 'General Strachwitz meant to put forward the condition of free withdrawal once more, but believed from the outset that it would not be granted'; 'on the 25th at 9 o'clock in the morning the commandant fetched' (the sentence continues on p. 382; 'holte ... ein', went out to meet and brought in); 'General Savary, who was accompanied by General Schramm and several officers, in, and led him to the Kommandantur [the commandant's headquarters]' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 381); 'for over an hour General Strachwitz strove to move General Savary to grant the garrison free withdrawal, but since all urging was in vain, he charged Major Dreßler to draw up the points of the capitulation with the French Captain Semery, which was then done with the participation of Major Colson and of Lieutenants Bismark of the regiment Prinz Ferdinand and Longe de Beauveset of the regiment Wedell'.

claims.value: Side A (French) attacked: Bodart has the French under Savary force the garrison to capitulate without a stroke of the sword. Höpfner: Savary set out against Nienburg on both banks of the Weser, the first patrols approached the town on the 24th, and that evening his parlementaire summoned the fortress to surrender; on the 25th the commandant negotiated with Savary, and after the parole the capitulation was made known and the bridgehead handed over; so on 26 November Nienburg too fell into the enemy's hands without any defence. No passage read describes any fighting at Nienburg.
claims.rationale: Coded A_attacked: side A approached and summoned the fortress and side B capitulated without fighting. The phase is left unresolved: Savary's move followed the capitulation of Hameln and orders the passages read do not give, while the summons and the terms were the commanders' own (claims side-a-command, side-a-objectives). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'General Savary, after leaving a garrison of 100 Frenchmen and 150 Dutch, set out on both banks of the Weser against Nienburg, so that on the 24th the first enemy patrols approached that town'; 'on the evening of 24 November a parlementaire of General Savary's brought the summons to surrender, with an account of all the well-known misfortunes of the Prussian army attached, and with the remark that insignificant Nienburg was surely incapable of any defence'; 'on the 25th at 9 o'clock in the morning the commandant fetched' (the sentence continues on p. 382; 'holte ... ein', went out to meet and brought in); 'General Savary, who was accompanied by General Schramm and several officers, in, and led him to the Kommandantur [the commandant's headquarters]' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 381); 'for over an hour General Strachwitz strove to move General Savary to grant the garrison free withdrawal, but since all urging was in vain, he charged Major Dreßler to draw up the points of the capitulation with the French Captain Semery, which was then done with the participation of Major Colson and of Lieutenants Bismark of the regiment Prinz Ferdinand and Longe de Beauveset of the regiment Wedell'; 'after the parole the capitulation was made known and the bridgehead handed over to the enemy at once. The walls remained occupied by the Prussians until the morning of the 26th'; 'so on 26 November Nienburg too fell into the enemy's hands without any defence'.

claims.value: Side B held a permanent fortress: Höpfner says Nienburg, largely razed soon after the Seven Years' War, was to some extent put in order again for defence in 1803, and that when Prussia took possession it was decided to restore the works so that it could withstand a three-week siege. The fortress formed a triangle whose southern side was covered by the inundation of the Aue; the north front had three polygons in a straight line, whose main wall was strengthened by a kind of tenaille, with no continuous covered way but two places of arms on its wings and a ravelin covering the Norder gate; the south front had two polygons, the main wall up to the half bastion at the Weser junction surrounded by a kind of counterguard, a ravelin covering the Lein gate and a hornwork before the half bastion at the upper Weser junction, again with no continuous covered way but 2 places of arms; the gorge was closed only by a palisaded wall, and all the works were of earth. A ravelin with wet ditches and a well-palisaded covered way served as bridgehead on the left bank; the valley heights overlooked it, against which cover had been sought by bonnets and traverses. Strachwitz had palisades set on the berm before the curtains and ladders fixed in the re-entrant angles for want of a covered way and posterns; to relieve the garrisons of the places of arms and the counterguard the men had to climb over the breastwork. The sluices, none of them quite tight, held well enough to give the main ditch its proper depth of water; each main work had small bombproof shelters; and on the whole the works could withstand a three-week formal attack. No passage read describes any works of side A.
claims.rationale: Coded B_fortified: side B held permanent works, readied before Savary's approach, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'Nienburg, situated on the right bank of the Weser, had been for the most part razed soon after the Seven Years' War, but in 1803, when the French took possession of Hanover, had been to some' (the word 'einigermaßen', to some extent, continues on p. 379); 'extent put in order again for defence' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 378); 'when Prussia took possession of the country it was decided to restore the fortifications so far that Nienburg could serve as a secure crossing over the Weser and withstand a three-week siege'; 'accordingly the fortress formed a triangle, whose southern side was washed by a small river, the Aue, which filled the ditches and flooded its whole left bank as soon as the mill on the south side of the fortress, between the town and the hornwork, was shut off' ('geschützt', read as the closing of the mill's sluice gates; our reading); 'this front was fortified by three polygons lying in a straight line, whose main wall was strengthened by a kind of tenaille'; 'a continuous covered way did not exist, but only two places of arms on the wings of the front, overlooked from the heights lying before it, and between the middle bastions a ravelin covering the Norder gate'; 'the south front consisted of two polygons'; 'the main wall up to the half bastion at the Weser junction was surrounded by a kind of counterguard. A ravelin covered the Lein gate; a hornwork lay before the half bastion at the upper Weser junction'; 'on this front too there was no continuous covered way, but only 2 places of arms before the Lein gate and the hornwork'; 'the gorge of the fortress was closed only by a palisaded wall. open_questions: Deferred: seen only in the OCR, a later letter of the Emperor to the Grand Duke of Berg in Foucart, Campagne de Pologne, t. I, pp. 241-242, which repeats that Nienburg has surrendered; the rest of Höpfner, Bd. 2, p. 383, on the war material lost in the campaign, not transcribed; General Savary's report and any order for the move on Nienburg, not found in the Foucart pages read; and the capitulation's text. No figure seen only in the OCR is restated.

Most consequential gap: side A's strength at Nienburg. Bodart's 6,000 is the only total, the figure he also prints for Savary's force at Hameln; Höpfner gives only the garrison of 100 French and 150 Dutch that Savary left at Hameln, and Mortier's observation troops of 13 November, weak and without a return, are not shown at Nienburg. A return of Savary's column, such as his report on Nienburg, could close it.

Disputes kept as separate claims or within them: the date (the capitulation drawn up on the 25th and made known after the parole, and the place falling on the 26th, Höpfner; 26 November, Bodart); the garrison (2689 infantry, 168 artillery and 54 hussars, together 2911, against a strength of 1500 for which the fortress was reckoned, Höpfner; 3,000, Bodart; under 1,500, the Emperor on 22 October; 10,000 at Hameln and Nienburg together, Mortier on 13 November); the guns (39 cannon, 10 howitzers, 2 mortars and 12 Wallbüchsen, Höpfner; 51, Bodart); the prisoners (the garrison into captivity, Bodart; the officers, the Feldwebel, some non-commissioned officers and married soldiers released, the Westphalians to be released at Minden and only the small remainder taken to France, Höpfner); and the burning of the town (a bombardment would quickly turn it into a heap of ashes, the council of war; its burning would not hinder the defence, Höpfner's description).
